rule: e1RM = weight x (1 + (reps + RIR)/30) (Epley with RIR); used for test scoring and for every prescribed load.
summary: Validation studies find reps-to-failure equations accurate at low rep counts and progressively worse above about 10 reps. In trained bench-press lifters, Epley gave small mean differences and the lowest standard error of the estimate among the methods compared, while other equations systematically under- or over-predicted. Accuracy is exercise-dependent: equations under-predicted 1RM in pulling exercises by 2-7 kg. The code has no cap on effective reps (reps + RIR), and adding RIR adds its own rating error. Proposed: Keep Epley, but when reps + RIR > 10 mark the e1RM as low-confidence: it does not set a new test result or raise working e1RM unless it is confirmed by a 10-rep-or-fewer set. Protocols stay at 3-6RM. Bump the code version in CODE_RULES. Possibly wrong if: the athlete's high-rep e1RMs agree with low-rep e1RMs within about 3% across a block.

sources.note: Resistance-trained adults, bench: Epley had small mean differences and the lowest SEE versus velocity, Wathen and Mayhew methods.
Reynolds 2006: the drop from 1RM with reps is non-linear; 5RM predicts best; use no more than 10 reps in linear equations.
Mayhew 1995 (n=220): equations had r 0.82-0.98 but over- or under-predicted, more so above 10 reps; Brzycki was most accurate at 10 reps or fewer.
Lat pull-down/cable row: rep equations under-predicted 1RM by 2.1-6.7 kg; velocity methods were more accurate.
